title: Why Thinking Belongs in the Language Classroom
brief: Open this section by drawing on the source's framing of critical and creative thinking as lifelong skills with broad applications inside and outside the language classroom. Explain the source's distinction between critical thinking (using reasoning skills to question and analyze the accuracy or worth of ideas) and creative thinking (new, alternative ways of looking at things that differ from the expected). Use the source's point that teaching techniques for critical thinking apply as well to language studies as they do to content areas such as social studies or science, and that teachers can combine all three — critical thinking, content, and language — in a single lesson. Close by noting the source's claim that open-ended learning can lead to cases where students become knowledge 'experts' and end up knowing more than the teacher about topics they have researched or explored.

title: A Hierarchy of Questions: From Recall to Creation
brief: Explain the source's distinction between factual questions and higher-order questions, drawing directly on the Observation Guide's description of how the Description section yields mostly factual, right-or-wrong information while the Prediction, Reflection/Opinion, and Extension sections elicit higher-order thinking. Use the source's vocabulary definitions of 'analyze' (examining something methodically by separating it into parts and studying their interrelations) and 'synthesize' (taking information or objects and combining them into a new form) to illustrate what moves up the hierarchy. Include the source's examples of question stems that open higher-order thinking: 'What if...?', 'Why do you suppose that...?', 'Imagine that X...', and 'Let's try Y...' Emphasize the source's point that factual answers are more likely to be right versus wrong in nature, while open-ended questions result in many right answers.

title: Open Tasks and the Many-Right-Answers Principle
brief: Focus on the source's core claim that critical and creative thinking means accepting more than one 'right' answer, and connect this to the source's definition of inquiry-based learning as an approach in which students learn about something or explore an issue through a series of open-ended questions. Draw on the source's three classroom activities — the synthesis warm-up, the group skit task, and the all-class simulation — as concrete illustrations of open tasks. Use the source's answer-key note that giving different groups different problems keeps everyone motivated and interested and is a way of sharing information and raising awareness across groups, with students effectively teaching each other. Contrast this with display questions, which the source implicitly frames as producing factual, single-answer responses, to show why open tasks generate richer participation.

title: Thinking Tasks in Action: Three Classroom Examples
brief: Walk through the three video-segment activities from the source as a sequence that moves from lower to higher cognitive demand. Describe the warm-up in which students synthesized collected information and reported on it — which the source identifies as good examples of higher-order or critical thinking skills — then the skit task in which students analyzed a problem, wrote a script, and performed it, and finally the all-class role play or simulation in which some thinking and language was structured (during planning) and some was unstructured or 'on the fly' (during the simulation itself). Use the source's observation that the simulation encouraged students to take on roles and present information in new ways, and that it encourages creativity. Highlight the source's summary question about what percentage of class time seemed devoted to strictly factual versus higher-order activity, prompting readers to reflect on their own ratio.

title: Why Thinking Tasks Produce Richer Language
brief: Draw on the source's framing that open-ended questions will result in many right answers, while factual questions end with true/false, yes/no, or one correct answer, to explain why thinking tasks generate more language output. Use the source's description of the warm-up activity as involving integrated language skills plus a variety of self-management and communication strategies to show that higher-order tasks naturally pull in multiple skill areas simultaneously. Reference the source's point that the teacher opens the way for students to put their curiosity to work and to pursue lines of questioning to which the teacher may not always have the answers — framing this as exploration together of knowledge frontiers — to explain why such tasks sustain longer, more authentic exchanges than display questions. Connect to the source's note that the Observation Guide itself functions as a critical and creative thinking activity, illustrating how even a reflective tool can model richer language use.

title: Building Thinking into Your Own Lessons: A Practical Action Plan
brief: Guide readers through the source's four-step action plan for integrating critical and creative thinking into existing lessons. Cover Step 1 (identifying a topic or upcoming lesson to enrich with critical thinking, starting small and experimenting), Step 2 (developing a set of extended questions to go with existing resources, using question techniques drawn from sources the module references), Step 3 (anticipating the directions students might take and planning for different students or groups to make different choices — skit, role play, poem, collage, and so on), and Step 4 (trying the questions in class, varying whether all students get the same questions, different questions, or choose their own, and then reflecting on what worked and why). Emphasize the source's framing that this need not take up a whole class period, making the approach accessible for any teaching context.
